utterances.text: Do you know that there were Bosniak members in that police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know that not long after that, it was along the ethnic composition that the police in Stolac was organised, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was organised, but what the actual composition was I don't know. I know there were Muslims in it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question because of the overlapping. The answer is:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were no Serbs. THE ACCUSED CORIC:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Were there Serbs in Stolac at all as citizens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, try and slow down a little, because the interpreters are having difficulty in following you. THE ACCUSED CORIC: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs came to the Stolac MUP perhaps a year or two ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were invitations to applicants for vacancies in MUP. If nobody applied, what could we do? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess that was so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I see that you have a good memory. When Stolac was liberated, do you know that the overwhelming majority in the HOS were actually Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually don't know those people at all. Croatian people, the HOS was just a foreign army for me; all people from Bosnia, Croatia, everybody mixed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a couple of months after the liberation of Stolac, so a while ago, I said there were -- the majority of those in Stolac were Croats. Do you know that a couple of months after the liberation of Stolac, this very same HOS had over 90 per cent of Muslims and the Croats had left the HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander of HOS was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know his nickname, not his name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Is his nickname Dugi, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: What did the people call him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prevalent opinion among the people was that he was a Croat. What he was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of an incident when this person, during a dishonourable military operation by Bosniak HOS members, had to use fire power against his own soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware. I was not in the army. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps if you described it in more detail, I could remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Did you read Mr. Dizdar's book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: This is described in the book. Can you remember now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I'm not quite sure what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: There are a couple of books. Which one did you read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this last one about half a year ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is all the questions I had to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The next lawyer, and then we will conclude. Just a minute. After that, the judge will be putting a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness BI, you have been asked whether you knew the names of certain persons who were perhaps not directly involved or also involved in setting the fire or being there, and then in the plundering and in transporting you, and you were then stopped from telling the names. Would you be so kind as to tell us these names. I think that the Chamber is interested in knowing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The expulsions and the plundering of money, gold, and other valuables was mostly done by Marijan Prce, whom I just mentioned, Vide Palameta, nicknamed Dugi; Boskovic, this is -- I don't know his first name. He was an inspector prior to the war in the MUP. His nickname is Celo. And that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has just a couple of questions that arise from either questions put by the Bench or by Mr. Praljak to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BI, you were asked about whether there were witnesses to the fires that you've described for us. Can you tell us, if you recall, at the time when these fires broke out whether there were significant numbers of people out and about on the streets of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people from the surrounding houses, predominantly women and children, went out, at least in front of their own doorsteps to see what was going on, but this was for a short while, ten or 15 minutes or so. The soldiers on the stairs that I referred to, they sort of deployed, if I can say so, and they actually returned all the people, sent all the people back into their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it might be helpful if the witness were again shown the bundle, IC 18, and he can indicate on that perhaps a couple of things that he's just told us about. If that can be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BI, you've mentioned several times in response, I believe initially to a question put to you by Judge Antonetti on page 35, line 16, you mentioned soldiers on the steps. Are the steps that you were referring to visible on the photograph, the first page of IC 18?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please point to the stairs that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the witness has marked the steps of the school with a circle. He's circled the steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, there was also some questions put to you by the presiding Judge concerning these two fires. Can you please point to where the first fire that you observed broke out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has marked a 1 on the roof of the mosque. And Witness BI, can you mark where the second fire that you witnessed on that day broke out, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now that you are dealing with this photograph, can you show us, please, on the photograph, the spot where you played soccer with your friends.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The spot can't be seen but I can describe it to you. It can be seen behind the school, or rather, it is behind the school, because within school, there is a playground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So it's behind the school. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, it was a bit unclear from the marking. Can you mark the spot where the second fire broke out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buildings are behind the trees. [Marks] But it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you place a number 2 there, please. Inside the rectangular box.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness BI.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before we conclude, I have a question which seems both relevant and useful to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the town of Stolac in 1993, were there any firemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes. They are there to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Based on the photograph, in addition to what can be seen there, can you point to us where the firemen were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see it on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it can't be seen, was it to the right, to the left, or in which direction, looking at this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in this direction, perhaps 150 to 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So in that direction. About 200 metres. On that day, you didn't see any firemen, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I may have been the victim to an error, but it seemed to me when you were first asked where the second fire had started, you pointed to a spot left of the minaret where the fountain pavilion is located. It is not really visible. It was between the trees. And then when you were asked again, after a discussion about another issue, the football, you pointed to a different spot, which is seen from here above or behind the mosque. Have I seen this wrongly? Are you sure which is the place where the second fire started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure about what I'm saying. I don't know how you see this photograph. What can be seen up here was a plot of land. This wasn't the playground. This is an old picture of Stolac. I don't know in which year it was taken. The playground is between these two spots, the school and the plot which later is the spot where they built another school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this has nothing to do with my question. My question concerns the immediate surroundings of the mosque. You were first asked to show where the first fire started, or where the fire first started, and you showed the scene from on the picture the part, yes, left of the minaret. Then you were asked where the second fire started, and you put the pencil a little bit more to the left still, which is, according to the plan, the place where the fountain is. Then came this intermezzo about the football field. You were asked again where the second fire started, and this time you put the pencil on the trees that are immediately behind the mosque as seen from here. I want to know where, where did the second fire start, really?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This black spot to the left of the minaret was placed there by me in order to mark the spot where I was, because that's how I understood the question, where I was when the second fire broke out. That's the spot that I marked. And it's right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could, just for clarification's sake, on the left side of the photograph, there are now two arrows pointing off of the photograph. Yesterday I asked the witness about where his house was and he drew an arrow off the map, and in response to your question just now he marked a second arrow where the fire brigade was. I would just ask if the witness could perhaps clarify that so we have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, there are two arrows. Can you put an H next to the arrow pointing to where -- or an A, let's mark it with an A, for where your apartment was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the arrow, the second arrow, can you mark that with an FB for "fire brigade."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, this concludes your evidence. The entire Trial Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague. I also hope that you will be able to find a job soon. This is the hope of the entire Trial Chamber. This doesn't depend on us, of course, but I wish you all the best in that regard. I will now ask the usher to lead you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, just a minute, sit down, please. First we need to put down the blinds because we have audience behind you. All right. You can leave the courtroom now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now turn to the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, what are you going to tell us about your last witness for this week? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness, my understanding, is ready to commence his testimony. His direct evidence will be led by my colleague Mr. Scott, assisted by Mr. Bos. At this point Mr. Kruger and myself will be taking leave of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Scott will now put himself in the front row. Very well. Mr. Scott, first of all, let me fix the timetable. We have another hour and a half remaining to our lunch break. We will have our lunch break at 1230, until 1400 hours, and then when we reconvene, we can work until 1715, and then we have the whole day tomorrow. Within that space of time we have to examine this witness. Let me remind you that the Defence must have the same amount of time as the Prosecution. Therefore, please tell me, how long do you expect to take with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My best estimate at this particular moment would be that we are looking at something around -- I'm going to say something around four and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Four and a half hours. That means that we need a total of nine hours for this witness. Which means that we may run out of time. Could you bring it down to four hours so that we are more likely to conclude on time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just can't make -- I'm sorry, I just simply cannot make that commitment. We are trying very hard to present this evidence to you as efficiently as possible. I think everyone in the courtroom will agree that Mr. Smajkic is an important witness. He is the most senior Islamic cleric in the Mostar region, was during the war and remains in that position today. He addresses a wide range of issues. I think the Chamber should have the full benefit of his evidence and we will do the best we can, but I just simply -- the alternative is to not present evidence to the Chamber that we believe should be presented. I don't -- would like to avoid that situation if possible. I will just say that we will do the very best that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Do what you can, but at any rate, if we don't finish with this witness tomorrow at 1.45, this witness will have to stay here until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I would ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's bring in the witness right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good morning, sir. Before you read out your declaration, would you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 9th of February, 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession currently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a mufti, a religious officer for the region of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before an international court or national court in your country, or is it the first time that you're testifying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in 2001 here, before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you testified in which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in the Tuta case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now I will ask you to read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. You can sit down now. Very well. Since you have already testified, you won't need a lot of introduction from me. First you will be answering the questions put by the Prosecution. You have already met them. The Prosecution indicated that they will be using four and a half hours for their examination, which means that you will be testifying today and tomorrow. And then the Defence teams are seated on your left, and they will be putting questions to you as well. They have the same amount of time. If we do not manage to finish by 1.45 tomorrow, unfortunately, you will have to stay here until Monday. But I am counting on the cooperation of both sides and hope that your testimony will be concluded tomorrow. All right. Since the time is already running, I will now give the floor to Mr. Scott, who has one hour to start with his examination. I will also like to ask the Registrar to see, to check with the interpreters, whether, if we do not conclude on time, we can stay a little bit longer. Please go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, you just heard there is some concern with some of the time schedule that we must deal with here. In order to move as efficiently as possible, I'm hoping there will be no objection if I lead you through some of your background information. I don't mean that out of any disrespect to you as a witness but simply to use the time most efficiently. Sir, it's my understanding that, as you just indicated, you were born on the 9th of February, 1947, in a town or village near Mostar but you've essentially resided in Mostar most of your life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you graduated from the theological faculty in Sarajevo. I didn't note down the year of that, but when did you graduate from the theological faculty?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I graduated from Gazi Husren-Begova Medresa in Sarajevo in 1965. And following that, I went to study in Iraq, where I graduated from the Baghdad University in 1971. I have a degree in the Sharia law and Arabic language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And since that time, after returning from your studies, you returned -- as I understand it, you returned to Mostar in approximately 1972 and you've been basically continuously employed in your religious functions in the Mostar area since 1972; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, sir, from 1972 to approximately 1980, you worked in various positions concerning, again, Islamic religious and educational work in the Mostar area, and during this time, you also acted as the deputy to the person who was the mufti at that time, Mr. Zufer Beslic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when the -- when Mufti Beslic died in 1975, you took over his duties in an acting capacity and then were officially appointed the mufti in 1980; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the testimony that brings you here today, you were also in this position of mufti during the time period 1992-1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you continue to hold the same position today; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mufti Smajkic, would you please tell the Chamber, assist the Chamber, please, with explaining what is a mufti, where does it fit into the Islamic religious structure, if you will, and give a brief description of your jobs and roles as the mufti of the Mostar region.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: A mufti is the main religious authority in a region. He is in charge, both directly and via municipal centres in his jurisdiction, of organising normal conditions for development of religious life and practice of religion under normal circumstances. He can achieve this by ensuring all the necessary preconditions for normal work, by ensuring proper funding, personnel, human resources, and infrastructure, that is to say religious facilities. Duties of a mufti include issuing guidelines for the work of municipal centres and contributing to the affirmation of religious values in the most proper manner. In this case, my competencies now cover three cantons; Herzegovina-Neretva canton, Liva canton, and Western Herzegovina canton, as well as the parts of the Republika Srpska, that is to say Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps it will assist the Chamber in terms of the geographic area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you've just described it, and the structure of the muftis if I ask you this question: How many muftis are there for the entire country covered by what is now Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, the office of mufti in Mostar includes Konjic, Jablanica, the seat is in Mostar, Capljina, Ljubuski, Livno, Tomislavgrad, Prozor, Glamoc, Stolac and Neum. These are the towns in the federation. As for Republika Srpska, it is Nevesinje, Gacko, Bileca, Trebinje and Ljubinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me come back in a moment to the question I asked you before, but in terms of what you've just said, would it be correct then to understand that during the period roughly 1992-1994, and when we talk about something that was then called either the Croatian Community or Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, were you the mufti at that time whose jurisdictional territory, if you will, would have included all of what was described at that time as Herceg-Bosna? Or if not, can you identify to the Judges any part of what was claimed as Herceg-Bosna that did not fall within your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Some of the towns mentioned did fall within my area of responsibility. However, the towns in Central Bosnia are in the jurisdiction of the Travnik mufti and partially Zenica mufti. Thus, we can say that Gornji Vakuf, Donji Vakuf, Kupres, and other towns in Central Bosnia are outside of the jurisdiction of Mostar mufti.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Generally speaking, then, we could understand and the Judges can correctly understand that your area of responsibility included what might be described as all of the Herzegovina region; is that correct? Not including Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes; for Herzegovina, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me go back to the earlier question I asked you: Again, just to put your overall structure in context, in this period 1992-1994, how many muftis were there covering the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That is, you said there were -- there was yourself in the Mostar region, there was a mufti for Zenica, there was a mufti in the Travnik area. How many muftis were there in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that time period, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Based on the previous organisational chart of the Islamic community, the one that existed before the war, there were four muftis and four regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, four mufti offices. One was in Mostar, one in Sarajevo, one in Tuzla, and Banja Luka. The one with the seat in Banja Luka covered the territory of Banja Luka and Krajina. And this is how it was organised and how it existed for decades. There was never any interruption in Mostar. There has always been a mufti seat in Mostar. In war, another four offices were set up in addition to the existing four. One was set up in Bihac, in Travnik, in Zenica and Gorazde, for Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, just in terms, sir, of your overall responsibilities again, can you tell the Judges, what is the nature of your role or responsibility, if any, in relation to the appointment or supervision of Islamic officials or clerics that fall within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Based on the regulations of the Islamic community, which are in force now, Reis-ul-Ulema, who is the highest authority and the leader of the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the proposal given by a mufti, appoints the main imams in municipal centres, in all municipal centres where the Muslims have an organised religious community. The local organs of the Islamic community appoint imams in djemat, which is our word for parishes. This is done by the local municipal organs of the Islamic community, which are called medzlis. Naturally this is also done on the basis of the approval given by mufti. Mufti is in charge of supervising the work and issuing guidelines to all the imams in his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just for the record to be complete, you mentioned this Islamic cleric official who was superior to you and would be the most senior Islamic authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What is the name of that position? I'm not asking now for the name of the person or holder of that position, but just as your title is, if I can say it that way, just as your position is called mufti, what is the name of that position?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Reis-ul-Ulema is the title. That's the supreme mufti in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We muftis compose the council for the Reis-ul-Ulema, and he's the supreme mufti in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And is his seat in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it also in Sarajevo during the time of the war?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I've asked you about your appointment and supervision of cleric -- Islamic clerics. Let me also ask you, as mufti do you have any role or responsibility related to religious buildings or properties that fall -- again fall within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I said that one of the main responsibilities we had was to create the necessary infrastructure for religious rites, so that means creating, or rather, building mosques and other facilities for the Islamic community, and thus protecting the facilities and buildings of Islamic communities is one of the responsibilities of the municipal bodies as well as one of the mufti's responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just to make it that a bit more concrete, if a local Islamic community wants to build a mosque in their area, their village, what have you, would you have some role in approving and supervising that process?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The local bodies would consult the mufti and the mufti would issue a certificate, or rather, approval, a justification for building a mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in connection with the topic that we will come to later in your testimony, could it also be said that if there is damage to a mosque or if a mosque is, in your area of responsibility is destroyed, would that information come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, moving forward, then, to some of the beginning parts of the conflict, is it correct, sir, that sometime in the first half of 1992, the Serbs -- Serb forces, the JNA, forces associated with the JNA, asserted control over the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Judges, starting in the spring of 1992, in approximately April, how that conflict developed in terms of the conflict at that time between Serbs on the one hand and the Croats and the Muslims or Bosniaks on the other?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The Jugo army and the Serbian troops arrived in the territory of Mostar in the month of September, 1992. They were there with the reserve forces and Herzegovina was then placed under the control of the then JNA. There were various acts of provocation, various incidents carried out by those forces that had full control over the territory that they had taken. There were various provocative acts. They would control traffic, carry out checks of the traffic and of individuals, they would open fire on certain buildings. They would also open bursts of fire directed at religious buildings and mosques. And this continued for several months, up until the month of April, as you yourself have said, the month of April in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, please? You said a moment ago, or at least it appeared on the transcript as, when I asked you the month, or when you gave a time, you said September of 1992. Did you mean to say September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then picking up on your last answer, this behaviour and these actions continued from approximately September of 1991 when they -- when the force -- JNA or Serb forces first appeared or at least asserted increasing control over that area, and continued until the spring of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges whether during this conflict in the first half of 1992, did many Muslim or Bosniak residents who were -- at that time had been living on the east bank, if you will, or the left -- the east side or East Mostar, the left bank, whichever terminology one wants to use, that many of these Muslims moved to the right bank during that time, during this conflict?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: They were preparing to liberate the town from the occupying forces, and while doing this, the Bosniaks in Mostar, together with the Croats from Mostar, prepared themselves to carry out a decisive strike, or rather, to liberate the town from these forces. Throughout the month of April and around the 8th or 9th of May, 1992, many Bosniaks crossed over to the right bank, to the western part of Mostar. I am aware of this because up until the 9th of May, 1992, I had an office in the eastern part of the town, and I was there until that date. By that time, these paramilitary groups, Arkan's men, Seselj's men, et cetera, had already been set loose. They were in the mahala area, in the centre, and that's the period of time during which the remaining inhabitants crossed over to the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we move on with these other events starting in the late spring of 1992, but just to put things in historical context, if you will, what did you understand -- by the spring of 1992, what was the status of the organisation -- the existence and operation of something that was then called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? It existed by that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was already in existence. It already existed in April, and later on in May the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna assumed control of the civilian parties of government in Mostar. They did this by carrying out a military putsch, we could say, and the HVO had both military and civilian power at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So not only did the Herceg-Bosna exist at the time, and it asserted control, and you knew at this time that something called the HVO was also one of the actors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mufti Smajkic, we are going to talk about these things in some greater detail in the course of the day, but would you give the Judges now a bit of an overview, if you will. You just said that by this time, there had essentially been a military putsch by which the Herceg-Bosna authorities, the HVO, had taken control of the government in Mostar. Can you tell the Judges how that was done?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Mostar were in a very difficult position. There was a Crisis Staff composed of the mayor, representatives of political parties, and other prominent individuals who also -- and this body also acted as a sort of assembly. So when it came to defending the town, pressure was exerted in order to ensure that the Croats, or rather, the HVO were made responsible for the defence. In a certain sense, a possibility was offered to other forces, to the Territorial Defence, to the incipient BH army, so that they could participate in the defence, whereas the HVO held a command role. Most of the parties involved, apart from the SDP party, agreed to having the HVO being made responsible for the defence of the town. However, shortly afterwards, when the HVO was assigned the task of defending the town and ensuring that the town was liberated, shortly after that occurred, it took over control from the executive body, or rather, it replaced the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago a Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff that existed in the spring of 1992, when was that Crisis Staff first established in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was established at a time that the town assembly could no longer function, because by that time the Serbs had already left the Assembly, the Assembly could no longer take decisions in an appropriate manner, and there was then a core cabinet including the mayor and representatives of political parties, the SDA, the HDZ, the SDP and certain other parties, and these people composed a Crisis Staff that had legislative authority and civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've said a couple of times now in the last few minutes that one member of the Crisis Staff was the mayor of Mostar. Who was the mayor of Mostar? Specifically now we are talking in the spring of 1992. In the April-May, 1992, period, who was mayor?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It was Milivoj Gagro, Mr. Milivoj Gagro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, how had Mr. Gagro come to hold that position?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He was elected in the first democratic elections that were held in 1990, the first democratic and legal elections held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, after you said there was this military putsch after which the HVO asserted complete control of the Mostar government, did Mr. Gagro continue to be mayor, or what happened concerning Mr. Gagro?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He was removed. He no longer played a political role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who replaced Mr. Gagro, essentially, as the mayor or the leading executive official in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He was replaced by Mr. Jadranko Topic, who was the president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by what process was Mr. Topic put into this position as head of the HVO government of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, this fits into the strategy that was used to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, into the strategy for turning Mostar into a Croatian town. It fits into the strategy used in other towns in which HDZ leaders wanted these towns to be part of Herceg-Bosna. So the government appointed this individual to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the record is clear, sir, when you say the government appointed the individual to that position, which government are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to Mate Boban and his government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You've said that it was agreed by most of the parties, not everyone, but there was an agreement in the spring of 1992 that the HVO would have command of the defence of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand that agreement or that decision to also authorise the HDZ or the HVO or the Herceg-Bosna authorities to take complete political and governmental control of all structures and processes in the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That body authorised the HVO, gave power to the HVO, and this implied that they should be responsible for military issues and for the liberation of the town of Mostar. It did not mean that they should assume civilian power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this decision to give the HVO the lead in the military defence of Mostar, this was reflected in a written document that was dated somewhere approximately the 29th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could have the assistance of the Registry to display Exhibit P 00180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I don't have a hard copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's on its way to you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you see that document now, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, if you can tell by looking at that document - and if you need to look at it in greater detail, say so, please - but is that a -- is that the document, the 29th of April, 1992, document which memorialised or reflects this decision for the HVO to have the military lead in the defence of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's the decision in question. However, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that in Article 8, under item 8, it says that the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Mostar must form a temporary executive board as soon as possible, which shall make sure that the bodies of the Assembly administration in the Mostar municipality function. That's one of the items. So giving this command role and making the HVO responsible for defence means that all the civilian bodies of power in Mostar were disbanded, were eliminated. So the civilian bodies of power in Mostar no longer continued to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you -- I'm going to take you, in fact, through a number of the specific paragraphs of the agreement. If you can first direct your attention to section II. Is it correct, sir, that is the basic language that talks about putting the HVO in charge of the defence of Mostar? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then going on to Article 3, is it correct, sir, that what was contemplated at the time was that the -- all of these bodies would continue to be multi-ethnic bodies comprised of both Croats and Muslims? I'm not asking you if that was the case but is that what was supposed -- in your understanding, what was supposed to happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may object at this point to the form of the question, to the extent that a foundation hasn't been laid. We can certainly read the document and draw some conclusions from reading the document not having lived through those events. The question is was this gentleman part of the drafting of this document, was he part of the Crisis Staff, did he have any involvement? If the answer is yes, then obviously he would be competent to testify as to what the meaning is in certain provisions or what was envisaged. Otherwise, I believe it is outside the scope of his knowledge and therefore he's not competent to answer those questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the witness can talk about what happened in the city of Mostar during this time. He's clearly one of the senior community leaders. I will not ask him to interpret the document per se but I'm putting the document before him in order to lead into the next series of questions and my question in fact is, is that in fact what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Mr. Scott, ask the witness to comment on the paragraphs, but don't lead the witness. If there is any light the witness could shed on some of the paragraphs, let him do so. If not, it doesn't matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Precisely my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in looking, directing your attention to the -- to what is the language in Article number 3, and as it's been pointed out, everyone in the courtroom can see that, but once you can see what that language is, can you inform the Judges in fact, based on your experience and observation at the time, was it in fact the case that the -- that Muslims comprised senior or important positions in either the Muslim -- the HVO military or the HVO government as it was set up, allegedly, under this decision?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This article spells out precisely that the Croatian Defence Council shall be constituted of members of the Muslim and Croatian as well as members of other peoples, but that was only a letter on paper, because Bosniaks and Muslims at that time, although they did take a significant part in the defence of the city, had no command posts, held no command posts. Not only did they not hold any command functions, but they did not have an equal status of a combatant relative to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask you to direct your attention next to section IV, and again if you would just see what that provision says, can you tell the Judges whether that in fact was the case? That is, was that what happened in practice?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: One can see clearly here that the command staff should have been balanced. However, the Muslim armed forces were not equal in the command staff, nor were they equal in respect of the other rights that the Croatian soldiers had. As a matter of fact, I can tell you that the Muslim population reacted. It did not approve the move of their representatives - and I think that this is important for me to say this - who affixed their signature to this document which is to invest the Croats with the exclusive role of defending the city and holding the command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me also direct your similar attention to paragraph numeral -- VI, and in particular the second sentence in that paragraph, or section. And again, can you tell the Judges whether that in fact was the case? Was the ethnic structure of these institutions, did it reflect the ethnic structure of the soldiers actually serving in these forces -- in this force?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No. The Muslims were neglected in this respect, totally. Disregarded, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to VII, did the HVO military, in carrying out its functions under this decision, subordinate itself and coordinate its activities to the Municipal Crisis Staff as it had existed in Mostar up to that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned, but to be very precise, I can repeat: The minute it was structured and organised in this fashion, it eliminated, it removed, disbanded the Crisis Staff from that moment and it no longer existed onwards. It actually assumed the competencies of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, before we leave this document, that we can see on the bottom part of the last page the persons who signed this document on behalf of the Crisis Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I believe this to be an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, before we move on, and in reference to perhaps there might be some of the persons who signed this document, by 1992 and continuing into 1993, did there come to be any group of Muslims who were identified as having a perhaps more pro-HVO orientation than others?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: From the very inception of the articulation of a joint strategy and defence, we noticed an inferior position of the Bosniaks and of the representatives of the Bosniak and Muslim authorities relative to the Croatian staff. So that one could immediately observe, especially in regard to the president of the SDA, Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, that he actually promoted Croatian ideas and that Bosniaks and the Muslims demonstratively and in different ways actually condemned his actions and his conduct. He especially featured in such activities. He especially -- he featured especially prominently in such activities, as did the team around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the gentleman here is using "Bosniak" and "Muslim." We heard yesterday from the witness, the term "Bosniak" for Muslims did not come into play much later. The way the testimony is coming it's as if we have two different groups, Bosniaks and Muslims, being discriminated or being abused by the Croats or the HVO. I would like the record cleared. What does he mean by "Bosniak" and "Muslim" at this particular time that we are talking about, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in my questions to you this morning, out of deference to what I understand to be your preferred term of "Bosniak," I have used both terms, "Bosniak" and "Muslim." For the purposes of the record, and since we are primarily focusing on the time period 1992-1993, would you be offended if I -- if we use the terminology "Muslim" for the purposes of today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I accept this. I think it is better in order to avoid any quandaries. I apologise. I -- simply something which figures in current terminology. What is used now is "a Bosniak." And then it was "a Muslim." That's why I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying that in your opinion, the terms "Bosniak" and "Muslim" are synonymous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you would say that there is no distinction to be made between these two terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No distinction exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's carry on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think we were talking about the position of Mr. Hadziosmanovic during this time. And my next question to you was going to be what positions or role did Mr. Hadziosmanovic have at that time, whether in the government or within a political party or what have you? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He was a leading Muslim politician. He was the president of the municipal SDA and regional SDA bodies. So that he had absolutely a predominant role in the creation of policy in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How is it, sir, that -- probably the question is already forming in the minds of people in the courtroom, that this senior SDA position -- politician, as you just said a moment ago, seemed to take positions that were increasingly out of step with most of the Muslims in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: At these elections at which Gagro was elected mayor, those in 1990, that is when the SDA party won the most votes from the Muslim people. The people from the Sarajevo headquarters brought him and placed him in that position, not knowing how anyone would turn out to be. This was a period of turmoil, of ferment, and we were just leaving behind the communist dictatorship, so people of this ilk of the civic orientation would not be aligned with national parties, so that the idea was, the hope was that people like Hadziosmanovic, actually hailing from a religious milieu, would actually fill the bill, the function of such a leader, very well, because his brother, Mustafa Hadziosmanovic, had served time, many years, in communist prisons, in the prisons of the communist regime. So it was -- he and his family were thought to be the promoters of traditional values upon which we would be able to further build our state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Probably not a major point but since you mentioned it and so the record perhaps can be a bit clearer, when you mention Mustafa Hadziosmanovic having served time in prison during the communist era, why was he serving time in prison?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, he was convicted as a Young Muslim. Actually this was the name of the group, this was the name the group dubbed itself. And they were held answerable for their ideological prejudices against the communist system. Alija Izetbegovic also belonged to this group, the president. So that the brother of Ismet Hadziosmanovic did time together with Alija Izetbegovic, and probably this is the connection. Of course they did not know Ismet, they just appreciated him on the basis of his brother's worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, going back to Mr. Gagro, I failed to ask you, and I don't think it was mentioned - if it was, I'm mistaken - what was Mr. Gagro's ethnic identity or affiliation?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro was of Croatian affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, I think, before we break for the lunch recess, sir. This group of people -- let me start over again. Did a group of persons form around Mr. Hadziosmanovic who formed any other political party or group that tended to be more closely identified with the HVO during this time in 1992-1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I'm very well acquainted with that situation, and we had serious problems because all Muslim associations at the time, they all had problems in terms of consistently representing the interests of the Muslims at the time. We observed that and we expressed this in different ways, namely that Mr. Hadziosmanovic was not courageous enough or possibly was not actually willing enough to represent the interests of the Muslims in the right and proper way but always accepted an inferior position so that the problems perpetuated themselves and actually grew without being resolved. You can see this from a document which reflects his practice. This is from September, 1992. You can see that Hadziosmanovic himself requested the HVO, on -- that we discuss in a democratic fashion and on a prompt basis certain problems which encumbered our overall relations, starting from the patches worn by the soldiers - we wanted them to be common ones - up to the establishment of joint institutions, resolving the question of the state flags, and so on and so forth. Not to belabour the point, this simply means that he himself was aware of this inferior position of the Bosniaks, i.e., Muslims, at the time, but it is quite possible that in this representation of his, he actually just did it so as to say that he had done something, but what he was actually doing in practice was to collaborate with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would -- I see the time. We would be moving on to another topic, so I suggest that we take the break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's half past 12, so we'll have our break. I've done some calculations. We should be continuing until 1745, which means, Mr. Scott, that at 1745, you will have concluded your examination-in-chief. Tomorrow Defence counsel will have the same amount of time for their cross-examination. We will resume at 2 p.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to go now to a time again in about April or May of 1992. Were you involved around that time in a television programme that was broadcast from Split, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I myself went there with Mr. Topic and I did appear on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that was about and how you became involved in that.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziosmanovic suggested that we should go to Split as part of a delegation, as part of a joint Muslim-Croat delegation in which the representatives, both Muslims and Croats, would discuss political matters, and I, together with the head of the bishopric, was to send an appeal for humanitarian aid to be delivered to the town of Mostar, that had been surrounded, that had been militarily besieged. In addition to Mr. Topic, we were accompanied by his brother, Marin Topic. I didn't know which Muslim politicians would be present, but when I arrived in the studio, I saw Mr. Salahovic there, who Ismet Hadziosmanovic had authorised to discuss political matters, and I, together with Mr. Luka Pavlovic, was supposed to issue an appeal for humanitarian aid. That was supposed to be done on that programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, sir, if you know, can you give us the first name of Mr. Salahovic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Amir Salahovic, who is a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you agree to go on this and participate in this programme voluntarily, did you believe you had a choice to do so, or what happened after being asked to do this?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I accepted this suggestion and took it to be one made in good faith. I thought that Mostar required aid and I thought that the politicians had their own work to do and that I, together with my colleague Luka Pavlovic, could be of use if we were seen together on television, if people could see that we had adopted a common front with regard to the aggression carried out by the Serb or Chetnik forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was the Catholic cleric, when you appeared on television, was he dressed in clerical clothing and were you dressed in your clerical clothing?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He had a priest's sign on him. It was wartime and there was an incident, since Mostar had been surrounded, and they would open fire on us. At night he fell out of the car. The conditions were wartime conditions so he couldn't really get dressed but he did have certain symbols or him that made it possible to identify him as a priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were travelling, in fact, to go to Split for the purposes of this presentation, did you have any trouble at the -- crossing the border into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: We, the Muslims, did have problems when it came to moving around freely. When attempting to obtain the necessary documents, Mr. Hadziosmanovic provided me with a piece of paper that bore his signature. That was supposed to be sufficient for my purposes. It was supposed to make it possible for me to move around freely, to circulate freely, since we were partners with the Croats. However, at the first check-point that we arrived at, and that was under the control of the HVO, I was sent back from that check-point and they requested that I provide them with a sort of identity document issued by the HVO. So I had to return that piece of paper signed by Mr. Hadziosmanovic. He was very angry, and he phoned someone from the HDZ who obtained a pass which enabled me to leave Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When the HVO check-point refused to accept the pass from Mr. Hadziosmanovic, did they make any further comment to you about that, about that pass?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to me to put this in very brutal terms, but they used a rather -- a rather vulgar vocabulary to describe the way in which that piece of paper could be put to good use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, you did, then, attend the programme. Was anything said during the televised programme about the Croat political plan or the HVO political plan at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at the studio, the situation I observed there is one that one could describe as a mobile situation. There was a certain euphoria. There were people who met Mr. Topic there, who greeted him in a particular way, and I didn't really understand what was going on at the time. However, when Mr. Topic took the -- when Mr. Topic took the floor, or rather, when he started speaking and when his image appeared on the screen, it said in subtitles that he was the new mayor of Mostar. So there was this atmosphere of euphoria. People in Split were euphoric because they believed that Mostar had finally become a Croatian town. The TV presenter asked Mr. Topic, "Who is your president?" And he said, "Mate Boban." He also asked me who my president was. I said my president was the elected president, Mr. Izetbegovic. A discussion ensued. They wanted us to accept the appointment that the HDZ supported, that the Croatian community supported, and it was even suggested that Sarajevo couldn't help itself. They suggested that we should join the Croatian people, that that's how we could save ourselves. At one point in time, Mr. Marin Topic joined the discussion and he said that Neretva was a viable option for us. In other words, that the right bank or the western side of the Neretva was an option for us, we wouldn't be fighting a Serbian aggressor on the left bank, and Mr. Salahovic was irritated by this. He was the official representative of Ismet Hadziosmanovic. He said he had to amend this statement because Salahovic had to return to Mostar, and when people heard what had been said, how would he be able to look them straight in the eyes? Because we were partners and we were supposed to fight for the liberation of the entire town. However, the statement remained such as it was. After the programme had been completed, Mr. Salahovic literally knelt down in front of the Topics and asked them to say that our common objective was the liberation of the entire town of Mostar, and you can do your -- draw your own conclusions as to what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the time that you were travelling to Split for the purposes of this presentation, did you have any idea that these political statements would be made, in terms of Mostar being a Croatian town and that this was all now -- had all now been accomplished and the statements that you've made to us in the last few minutes? Did you know that that was the presentation that was going to be made?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I knew nothing about that. It was a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you -- were you aware around this time, around this same time, in May of 1992, that there had been a meeting in Graz between Mate Boban and Karadzic in connection with something called the Graz Agreement?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. However, with regard to what I myself experienced, what army units experienced with regard to the events that took place, with regard to all positions and the enthusiasm that existed for the liberation of the town, I would say that all this indicated that something on a large scale was taking place, and that there was an agreement in the offing, and we have seen that that played a role in that approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you hear around this time that apparently the concept that had been discussed and agreed between Mr. Boban and Mr. Karadzic was that the Croats would have everything on the west side of the Neretva and the Serbs would have everything up to the east bank of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Topic's statement was confirmation of that, because I think this programme was broadcast via satellite, and they wouldn't even carry out minor acts or acts of minor importance without central authorities in Zagreb being aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where -- what was your understanding and the understanding of your Muslim colleagues and associates at that time as to where that left the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an integral part of the policies pursued at the time, and of the political statements; the right bank was to be Croatian and the left bank was to be Serbian, whereas the Neretva River was to be left to the Muslims. That was a well-known definition, or well-known saying at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing, sir, to move forward in May and June of 1992, can you tell the Judges a bit more. In the course of these events, what more was done in terms of the HVO takeover in Mostar? What other sorts of things did you see that illustrated that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, later on, the policies remained stable. The policies pursued followed their own course. The policies were flexible, in fact, and adapted to the situation that prevailed at the time. So at that time this was the idea that was put forward, a division on the basis of the Neretva River. Later, the HVO forces and the Muslims combined their efforts to defend and liberate the town. This was done under the command of Mr. Jasmin Jaganac, whom Tudjman sent to Mostar as the Croatian soldier or Croatian officer. This was probably done so that all the Muslims, without exception, would join the HVO units. And thus, the combat capacity of the Muslim units would be weakened. However, the purpose was to liberate the area. There was a new situation, a new reality, and by joining forces we managed to liberate the town. However I must point out that when the left bank fell, we weren't assisted, or rather, when the Chetnik forces took the left bank and when the JNA took the left bank, it was only Muslim forces who fought on the left bank before crossing over to the right bank. They were rarely assisted by individual groups or individuals who had friends fighting in the Muslim ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there has already been discussion in this case about the HVO and the Croats liberating Mostar. Can you please tell the Judges, were Muslim soldiers and were the Muslim side equally involved in the liberation of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Our fighters were completely equal. And they had a lot -- their morale was higher and they were more enthusiastic when it came to carrying out operations the purpose of which was to liberate the town. They were quite surprised when their role was a role that others wanted to minimise. They wanted the Muslim forces to feel that they were dependent on the Croatian side, on Croatian military capacity. They wanted them to feel inferior in this respect, and there were many incidents that actually revealed what was secretly being planned. So when it came to liberating Mostar and the wider area of Herzegovina, well, there were certain changes, or rather, this idea according to which the town of Mostar should be divided on the basis of the Mostar [as interpreted] became slightly modified. They wanted to base the territorial division on the way in which the territory was divided at the time of the Banovina. So when the Croatian forces arrived at the boundaries of that territory, they didn't want to go any further. Our fighters weren't aware of this. They could have taken more territory, they could have pushed on, but they didn't have the support of the Croats. So it means that there was a new agreement that had been reached between Tudjman and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of what was happening in the city of Mostar itself after the liberation, can you tell us what happened in terms of the city institutions, names of streets, the sorts of things that happened during this time.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: All institutions - the police, the courts, the schools, companies, et cetera - they were all called Croatian institutions. None of those public buildings or state buildings had the Bosnia and Herzegovina flag flying from it. They had the flag of the Croatian community flag flying from it. And the Muslims were expelled from all companies. No Muslims held any positions any more. So the town was quite simply covered in Croatian flags. I was an eye-witness of the situation. There were certain people who protested against such a situation. There were some young men who made these flags that had lilies on them and they would put them up on buildings, but they met with fierce resistance on the part of the police, the army, et cetera. So when this joint action was carried out to liberate the town, at certain elevations from which the Serbian forces had been pushed back, the Croats would plant their own signs or flags there. They wouldn't allow the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be planted at those positions but they did allow the planting of religious flags. So wherever there were flags with the crescent and star at various mosques, I know that these soldiers appeared there and collected all those flags. They could then say that wherever they had put up their own flags, that meant that they had liberated the territory, not the Muslims. That meant that they would only recognise us as a religious community, as a minority community, but not as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, it may be well known in the record at this point, but when you say the flag with the lilies on it, that is the flag of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened to the name of the post -- the Mostar post office?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, it was called the Croatian post office. The name was changed, and that was the case when it comes to other institutions too. The same prefix, the prefix "Croat," was used for all these other institutions. If I can add a humorous touch, we said that only the air has remained untouched by these policies. How will they claim that the air is Croatian too?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened around this time in terms of the educational programmes, the curriculum in the schools and how that was affected, if it was, by these changes.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Of course this was also -- this also affected the schooling system, all walks of society, the health system as well, from which Bosniaks, i.e., Muslims, were expelled. They had to swear allegiance to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna if they wanted to stay on in the surgeries, in the hospital. This was not too visible publicly, but the attempt at imposing the Croatian language on the Muslims as their official tongue actually met with vehement reactions on the part of educational workers, the children and their parents, and needless to say also on the part of the Muslim association, because the report cards, the diplomas at end of school year were actually as a rule, as an obligation, made out in the Croatian language for all the children, and we didn't want to accept that. The certificates they issued, the diplomas, were also stamped at the bottom, actually bore a Croatian symbol, which you can show on the screen, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: And that was also proof of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the Exhibit P 09492 please be displayed. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is this the -- what we might call a report card or certificate, an educational certificate or report that you've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of such a certificate, precisely. It says clearly on the top, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," and you can see in first place of the curriculum, you have first of all the Croatian language. And taught to a guy called Muamer Omerika, the son of Adem, and his first subject taught is the Croatian language, and this is, of course, against his will. And generally, it runs against our freedom to opt for a name for our own language, the language that we want to speak, and against segregation in our schools. And, of course, at the bottom you can also see the sign of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna without the sign of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the symbol of Bosnia and Herzegovina appearing anywhere on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was my next question to you, sir: Were any similar forms used in the schools at the time or made available through the Herceg-Bosna or HVO government that, instead of the Croatian chequerboard, had instead the signs, the symbols of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do not like to interrupt my colleague but what the witness was talking about was not shown wholly on the screen. So I should like to have this noted. So if you can scroll down the document on the screen so that we can see, indeed see all the rows, because the first line actually indicates something else. We didn't see this, what the witness was talking about, actually. [In English] No, no, reverse. The top of the document, and the witness is starting with reading first two lines and not the first line which says "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not sure if that's a question or a comment, but we can go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my dear colleague, the witness was reading what he saw, and he saw only "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," without the first line. So it's simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Perhaps the witness can explain this, explain the fact that in the heading of the document, we can see that it says the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is what first appears in the heading. What could he say in explanation of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did mention, however, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at page 86 of the transcript, line 1, what the witness clearly says, "It says clearly on the top Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." So I think there has been a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us whether, in connection with these issues and the Croatian language, the Croatian so-called curriculum, did you ever raise these issues with any leaders of the HVO government or structures?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Actually, we had constant contact of our political representatives and people from the institute of pedagogy, who were in charge of the educational system and who pointed out shortcomings of this nature and generally this defective practice of the wholesale overtaking, taking over of curricula with the content being applied in the Republic of Croatia. However, that bore no fruit and that is why the people then just boycotted school, or rather, instruction at that time. Our workers, our educational staff, our teachers, Muslims, boycotted instruction for about 15 days because they did not want precisely this to happen, to have in the report cards of our children it being written there that they were being taught the Croatian language. But no one paid any attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On this topic, did you ever have a meeting with Jadran Topic and Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, we had a number of meetings with Mr. Topic, and as I have already said, also with some other representatives, but it was like talking to a deaf person. And when this exercise proved futile, SDA representatives, Mr. Zijad Demirovic, organised a meeting with Mr. Prlic on one occasion, as well as with Mr. Filipovic, and I also attended that meeting. The intention, our intention, was to present the subject matter to a person who would actually exhibit understanding for our position, for our position in regard of this issue, from the standpoint nationality, of maturity, of identity, et cetera, so Mr. Demirovic organised this and Mr. Sefko Tinjak and Adem Omerika were also present, and a discussion along those lines was indeed conducted. However, Mr. Prlic failed to appreciate, to comprehend, our requests. Rather, he told us, "My language, too, is the Bosnian language." And then I replied to him, "Why don't you call it the Bosnian language, then? Why do you call it the Croatian language? Whereas you deny me that equal right to call my language the name I want to call it on the basis of my free choice without any coercion?" He then replied we could call it the Muslim language but not the Bosnian language. And, of course, we saw that as some sort of a ploy because of course there does not exist a Muslim language. There is the language of the liturgy, there is the language of the prayer, which is, of course, in our case, Arabic as is the case with Latin in the Catholic church and, of course, we wanted to have what other nations have, which is a name for their nation and their own name for their own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The changes that were taking place in the, what we might call the elementary schools, the schools prior to university, did you see or did you become aware of similar changes being made at the university in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The same things, exactly the same things, were happening at the university.
