Literally, courses were detached from Mostar, from the Mostar curriculum, to be delivered to other -- in other centres; in Siroki Brijeg or Neum. The curriculum was changed, the teaching faculty, the administrations echelons were also changed. There was this so-called Croatisation at the university, with people being appointed on that basis. If there were any Muslims that in a way exhibited a certain subservient attitude towards the Croats and teachers who actually advocated these ideas, the Bosnian patriotic ideas, they would be removed. So the latter group would removed from the university, in contrast to the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, sir, to your knowledge, did Jadranko Prlic have any role in these events at the university, the changes at the university in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Of course, he had to have a role. First of all, he was a professor at that university and then he was active on the political scene as a prominent member of the HDZ. Therefore, he was a person that had an impact on the overall political events in place and generally relations between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was the name of the university changed during this time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Not yet at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it changed at some point? And if so, tell us when.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: When open conflicts broke out, or rather, with the strikes of the Croatian army and the HVO against Mostar, and we can freely say Bosnia and Herzegovina, when that happened, all the staff and all the resources were expelled from the west side, or bank, and in those buildings, in those places, in their stead there was formed a Croatian university. Simply speaking, Muslim intellectuals, the teachers, the professors, were simply driven out of there, and by way of war booty, this infrastructure, the entire university, was converted into a university -- Croatian institution, a Croatian university, whereas the Muslims had to create another university of their own, starting from scratch. And they did, of course, the Muslims did establish a new university, and I have information that they -- they are actually suing the Croatian authorities for having usurped the joint university premises which they used to share with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the name of the university prior to the Croat takeover of the university?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It was the Dzemal Bijedic University.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How long had it had that name, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It would have been its 30th -- it is its 30th anniversary this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the name of the university after the HVO takeover?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It was called the Croatian University.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as these events unfolded, did the Muslim community and the leaders of the Muslim community attempt to make any response or make any protest to the various changes that you've told us about this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: These were, I can openly say, just mild reactions. Because they actually resulted in no changes. Because basically the situation persisted. And it was generally, I could say, quagmire, because nothing changed and the Croatian side actually stuck to its programme and intended to see it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the Registry's assistance to display Exhibit P 00318. When you've had a chance to look at that document, sir, can you tell the Judges what this document is and the circumstances that, to your knowledge, led to the preparation and sending of this or transmission of this document.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I can say that we actually turned in a vicious circle and were unable to make any headway. Not only in regard to the educational system but in regard to any agreement whatsoever. We can see, having said that, on the basis of this document, that the Muslims sought to initiate a dialogue, to initiate a substantive dialogue, in order to resolve those matters in an efficient way. So this deals with the question of information, with the issue of the university, of military units, the issue of participation in different businesses, economic enterprises, resources where, simply speaking, the Muslims had no access. So that political tensions kept mounting and they threatened to result in outright conflict and that is why we drew up documents of this kind, precisely in order to preclude that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so that those in the courtroom can have a broader view of the document other than just what's on the screen at the moment, could the Registry please scroll down, go to page 2. Of the English -- yes, excuse me, the English version. In terms of the, just as by one example, in the second paragraph that begins on page 2, at least in the English version, and I'm sorry, if you find the paragraph, sir, on the second page, it says, "The relations established on --" on yours it's not the second page, excuse me. In Article 1 or section I it says: "The relations established so far in carrying out war operations and successes against the enemy oblige us to arrange our relations in such a way so as to enable a permanent joint life of the Muslims and Croats in these areas." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that during this time, the Muslims continued to try to find ways and to have meetings and find ways to, as you described it here, have a joint life with the Croats and Muslims together?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: But that -- that is correct. Namely, we tried constantly, insistently, even accepting a degree of humiliation, I have to say, even accepting a humiliating treatment in all these negotiations. We accepted all that simply with a view to removing all --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, after the part that I just referred you to just now, it makes reference to the fact that no agreement was reached during talks. Do you see that, sir? Do you recall which talks or negotiations were being referenced by the document at this time? This is in July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: In that period since Mostar and the immediate vicinity of Mostar were a liberated zone and the liberated city and it was supposed to function with a new dynamics, for that purpose, the Muslims wanted to enter into an alliance with the Croats and continue liberating Bosnia and Herzegovina farther afield. However, no talks with the Croatian side were possible because they had gained what they wanted so that any further talks on the continuing the process of liberating territory was out of the question. And, of course, problems of this kind, like the one with the university and the recruitment, the employment of Bosnian and Herzegovinian Bosniak experts on work that they could discharge, that was something that the Croatian nomenclatura actually did not accept because suitability, correctness was the main criterion and not the actual capacity, knowledge and ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there are other aspects of this document that I would like to ask you about, but because of time constraints let me just ask you to look at the bottom of the original of the document, the B/C/S document, and can you assist the Judges, since it's a copy, and maybe difficult for all of us to read, can you identify to the Judges the three people and organisations -- excuse me, the four persons and/or organisations which signed and put their seal on this document.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The first seal is the Party of Democratic Action seal or stamp, and it is signed by Ismet Hadziosmanovic. The second one is of the Islamic community, and it bears my signature. The third one is of the Cultural Community of Muslims, Preporod, "Renaissance," and it is signed by Mira Rajic [phoen]. The fourth is the Merhamet, Muslim charitable society, signed by Sahovic, Izet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mufti Smajkic, it's just been pointed out to me that in the transcript, at least, the name of the third person may have been misunderstood. Could you state again the name of the third person who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Miro Mahmutcehajic. It's Miralem, and Miro for short, Mahmutcehajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have the Registry's assistance to go to the next exhibit, P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I have a question I'd like to put. The document that you signed, since you said that beneath a second stamp we can see your signature, this is a document in which the relationship between the Croats and the Muslims is being regulated, is being organised. If I've understood this correctly, none of the four signatories is a Croat. So how do we draft a document that organises the relationship between the two parties if all those who signed the document in a question come from just one of the sides? How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that these are simple matters, in fact. The signatures on this paper are of Muslim associations, the basic, the chief Muslim party, political party, the SDA, the Islamic community, the cultural society, the Preporod, and the charitable society, which is tantamount to the Caritas. This is the Muslim Merhamet. This is a collection of associations offering their perception of things to the Croatian side in order for the latter to consider it with a view to overcoming the accumulated problems related to humanitarian aid and intercepted convoys, the operation of the cultural society, of the Muslims, where their scope for media activity is being restricted, and the problems of the Islamic community because of their restricted freedom of movement - and we saw the check-points that we had to -- where we had to present our papers as humiliating and were prevented from passage on various occasions - and then you also have the party leader, Ismet Hadziosmanovic, who was with us in this exercise all the time, because he could not actually challenge the fact that these things were indeed encumbering our relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened to this document? What did the Croats do with regard to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing changed. Absolutely nothing changed. They ignored our document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may assist, before we move on, if the Registry could show the top part of the B/C/S document. The language at the very top of that page. Not the title of the document but there is the very first three lines at the very top of the page, sir, perhaps you could read that and we could get the assistance of the interpreters as to what that language indicates. The text on the very top.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see. I didn't realise that I was expected to read it. So: "Proceeding from the platform of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in conditions of war, and the platform for the united defence of the sovereignty and statehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the protection of the Muslims in Mostar and Herzegovina, we hereby lay down the premises for the regulation of current political relations between the Croats and the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. If we could then move on to Exhibit P 00374. Can you tell the Judges what this document is, Mufti Smajkic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the previous one, and the platform for the regulation of relations -- of sound relations between the Muslims and Croats and the protection of the interests of the Bosniaks, proceeding from that we undertook constant activities with a view to the promotion and harmonisation of relations between Muslims and Croats. Along those lines, we drafted this resolution of the Muslims of Herzegovina which, to a certain extent, defines our views on life, on cohabitation, on joint life, and issues a number of guidelines to combatants in terms of how they should fight honourably, without abusing a time of war for dishonourable purposes, and we defined the strategic thrusts for the Muslims who are in favour of a sovereign Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with, of course, envisaging the equal treatment under all internationally recognised conventions and such equal treatment being recognised also to all the people, all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whilst naturally condemning massacres and the already-observed examples of abuse, massacres, persecutions of people on a religious or ethnic basis, which did happen and in the city of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, I believe the Judges have already seen this document so I'm not going to spend much more time on it. I just wanted to establish that you were also involved in the preparation and signature or approval of this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I played an active role in the drafting of this resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask for the assistance of the Registry to please go now to Exhibit P 00375. And if you have that, sir, again can you look at that document enough to see what it is and tell the Judges what you know about the topic or issues presented in this document.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This document - and let me not take too much of your time to read it - is about refugees who had been accommodated in different spots in the city of Mostar while their status of refugees had been abolished and they were being prepared to be transported to areas which ostensibly were Muslim areas, without a say on the part of the people affected. Of course, this fits into the concept, the political concept, of the forcible creation of ethnically pure provinces. Of course, this could not but be attended by suffering, by an ordeal, and unfortunately, blood too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, sir: Just now you said it was about the refugees -- excuse me a moment. You say about refugees and then go on to say and they were being prepared to be transported to areas which ostensibly were Muslim areas. Which refugees were being transported?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Actually transports, convoys were being in preparation to transport Muslims who had been expelled from the area of Eastern Herzegovina by Montenegrin units, war units, and who were temporarily, who had temporarily taken refuge in Mostar, from Gacko, Bileca, Trebinje. And Nevesinje. And they were supposed to be transported to Zenica in Central Bosnia, where the population was predominantly Muslim. And I was engaged on that activity with our colleagues from our charitable society, the Merhamet, that took care of these refugees. And we asked the UNHCR office in Split to intervene. So they came and they postponed this operation or this actually vile intention from being carried out of transporting people to the unknown, people who had already gone through an exodus. And this indeed falls well within -- fits well within this concept of the expulsion of people and the forming of pure ethnic areas. And, of course, this was also intended to -- for the Muslims to actually prepare themselves for this, for the fate that the HVO authorities had in store for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In August of 1992, sir, when this document was prepared, as indicated on the bottom of the document, were Croat refugees also coming to Mostar from various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It's good that you've reminded me of that. It happened a long time ago and naturally one's memory fades. The Serbs had been ordered to leave Mostar because such was the agreement. There were many abandoned flats and the refugees in most cases found accommodation in those empty flats. However, the Croatian policies pursued at the time had a different objective. They wanted the Croatian population from the Central Bosnia and other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be transferred to these areas in which they would have the most power, and the term used is a notorious one; humanitarian transfer or relocation, and you can imagine what that meant, since these people had to leave the areas in which they used to live and be moved to a foreign area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question very directly, sir: When the proposal was being made to transport the Muslim refugees to Zenica, was there any similar proposal to transfer Croat refugees out of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I haven't heard about any such proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you mentioned this earlier today, sir, but throughout this time, or in 1992, a large number -- is it correct that a large number of Muslim men continued to participate in the HVO military? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It was a large number. There was a large number because in a certain sense they were privileged. They had salaries and they would receive parcels. And naturally, the ABiH didn't have much equipment or weapons, and they received no compensation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, did the Muslim members of the HVO ever propose a patch, a shoulder patch or insignia that contained both Croatian symbols and Muslim symbols?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: From the time that they started establishing the army and the HVO, the units, this was a problem that one encountered. So-called Muslim army couldn't understand or failed to understand that insignia is just as important as joint combat against a common enemy, a common aggressor. However, the Croatian side adopted Croatian insignia and did all it could to prevent the army from forming. They wanted everything to be done within the framework of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was a patch ever prepared that showed both symbols of Croatia or the HVO and symbols -- and I probably should correct myself, should not have said the Muslim army but the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the symbols of that state?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, people created these symbols. They tried to make sure that these common symbols were adopted, but it was useless. They quite simply wanted the army to be subordinate to the HVO from the very beginning. They didn't want any other military formations to exist outside of the HVO. In a certain sense, they tried to reduce these other forces to a minimum, or rather, to eliminate them completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did the HVO armed forces ever agree to use -- to your knowledge, ever agree to use a symbol or insignia, a patch, that contained both the symbols of Croatia or Herceg-Bosna and the symbols of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that at one point these symbols were agreed. However, this agreement was never implemented. And only after the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Accords, and once the defence component was unified that it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 00477. Do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what this document is, a letter dated the 14th of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what we just spoke about. This now takes us to September, 14th of September, 1992. This document continues to discuss the common symbols in the army. You can see in the continuation of this document. They were still discussing the adoption of common emblems of the army and Croatian Defence Council. Additionally, the Muslim side requested joint engagement of the HVO and the Muslim army, in order to commence with the final liberation -- this is towards the end of the text. I'm familiar with this text. Liberation of the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this letter, they say that a whole series of system errors need to be overcome in order to ensure democratic negotiations and improvement of the military and political situation in Mostar. This means that the situation there was constantly a tense one. This was signed by Mr. Hadziosmanovic, and he believed it necessary to ask that the HVO remove the obstacles placed before the army and the Muslim people. In item 1 it says through joint --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment, because again not everyone in the courtroom can scroll through the entire document, so if I could ask the Registry now show the second page of the English version so other people in the courtroom can see that, I'll just get -- I'm just going to pause a moment, sir, just so people can see more of the document.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the Registry now please go to page 3 for the English document. And please go then to page number -- at the bottom of page -- or go to page 4, please. And we'll see at the bottom of page 4, is it correct, sir, that the letter essentially has 15 numbered paragraphs or items of -- express -- raising various issues or expressing various concerns, correct -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think you have the full -- do you have the last page in front of you, sir, with the signature, the signature page? And if the Registry could please go to the last page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Signed by the president of the Regional Board of the SDA, Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you can just pause one moment, sir, I'm waiting for the English. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, we do not have the English text of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the hard copy, Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't have the hard copy and I thought it was supposed to be on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I think it's come up now. I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Not on mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology to Judge Trechsel for any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On this page, sir, you've already indicated, I believe, that it was signed by Mr. Hadziosmanovic, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't mean to interrupt. If we look at this document, there is no signature, and if you scroll all the way to the very first page, Mr. President, in English it says "copy" but I believe it's something different in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was awaiting for that remark. There seems to be a faxed message. Mr. Scott, what is the source of this document? There is no signature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honour, I misspoke when I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Instead of "signature," I should have said over the name of, prepared in the name of, Mr. Hadziosmanovic is what the witness testified to a few moments ago. The source of the document? I'd have to look at it on our witness list -- or excuse me, the exhibit list. The source of this document is Mr. Smajkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could read and have it translated, the very first part where it says "copy in English," I'm told that that's not what it says in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy to ask the witness to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, or Mufti Smajkic, if you could look at the first page of the original B/C/S document or the document you have in front of you on the screen, on the very first page, up toward the -- I don't know, you might say to the right of the letterhead, do you see a letter -- do you see a word -- could we get --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your microphone did not --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It says here, "prepis," which is a transcript or a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it copy or is it rewrite? Copy is something that is copied. Or has it been rewritten?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, since you are the person supplying this document, tell us, please, how did you come into -- how did you find this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document where we, the intellectuals, people who were members of these associations, had a meeting with Mr. Hadziosmanovic. I was present at the meeting, and you will see in the penultimate paragraph, it says that there should be freedom of movement for clerics when performing religious ceremonies. That was one of the remarks that we made to Mr. Hadziosmanovic. This took place in his meet -- in his office. Representatives of several groups came to see him, and in the form of this letter, he wanted to address all institutions of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna so that all of the matters mentioned here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the objection of the Defence was about something else. Even though we may be wasting time, can we please see what this is all about. Mr. Karnavas says this is a copy. Can you tell us whether the original of this letter was signed by Mr. Hadziosmanovic and whether it was sent to the HDZ, to the president personally, and were other copies, without a signature, sent to everybody else, including yourself? Is that the answer to the question as to whether this is a copy or transcript or an original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that's correct. This is what I received from Ismet, without a signature, whereas he sent to various other addressees, letters with the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We have the answer here. Counsel, exercising due diligence, should have extricated this answer from the witness himself. Please go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was about to ask the witness before this started in terms of the people on the bottom left side, or the lower left side of the document, are these all the people that, to your knowledge, copies of this letter were provided to? That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. He's unable to say that. He can say that their names are on the paper. How can this witness say that they were actually provided with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He may know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question should be does he know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Scott, please continue. We are wasting time without a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mufti Smajkic, during this time, to your knowledge, were a number of communications prepared by representatives of the Muslim community, the Islamic community, that were then transmitted to a number of the leaders of the HVO, of the Herceg-Bosna government, expressing the issues and concerns that were important to the Muslim people during this time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: A number of letters were sent to various addressees. I can tell you that a number of them were sent to the government in Mostar because that's where we were continuously. It had to do with the freedom of movement of clerics who were stopped at check-points. It had to do with religious ceremonies and the premises where they were to be carried out. We had serious complaints about the accommodation for the clerics, and me personally. We were housed with the refugees in a students' dormitory. I had a room three by four, and there were several hundred families living there around me. This in itself speaks clearly about the attitude that they had. We spoke about the university, education, army, and this reflects the attitude they had towards the clerics, religious individuals. It was all right to place a mufti in a room three by four while simultaneously they were building fat palaces. We certainly didn't mind that the bishop built a palace for himself. Of course, it was normal for him to have a decent premises, but this was again an example that reflected the attitude of Croatian authorities towards us Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. And this would be an appropriate time to take the afternoon break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you testified before the break about the inadequate office space that was provided to your office as the mufti for this Herzegovina region, and did you receive a letter back from the mayor of Mostar, Jadran Topic, concerning that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I received a letter, a threatening letter, one could say. In my correspondence with the bishop, I said that he had received a building which was a building of the very prominent Muslim citizen in the past, and that it was an illegal act. However, the bishop replied to me, saying that this building was given to him by the authorities and that he had a lot of respect for the authorities and for what they did. Mr. Topic, in his letter, threatened me, saying that I may not call the authorities illegal authorities, and I should focus on religious issues and leave the politics alone. So what I described earlier continued to persist. There was a constantly offending attitude of the representatives, both political ones and military ones, with respect to the Muslims. This means that in each area of life, it was left to the people to decide how they were going to act, without any regard for what kind of treatment we actually deserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P 00731. Can you tell us, sir, is that the letter from Jadran Topic that you received in response to your inquiry and that you have testified about in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward, because of the time concerns, sir, can you tell us, did you and other leaders of the Muslim community meet with President Izetbegovic in November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what happened at that meeting and the results of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic came to Mostar, intending to help in improving the relations between the Muslims and Croats, to alleviate problems. Also, he wanted to meet with representatives of Muslims, organisations, political parties, in order to see what needed to be changed, what needed to be improved, in order to ensure peace and a good quality life. I personally did not attend those meetings but I asked for Mr. Izetbegovic to see me, together with several other people. We received a message that we should come to the seat of the SDA, to the offices of Hadziosmanovic, and that Mr. Izetbegovic would see us for half an hour, that that was how much time he could spend with us. In that conversation, we informed him of the entire situation, of the degree of serious problems we were facing, the problems we had with the authorities which had driven out from that territory anything that symbolised the former state, and we also informed him about all the regulations that had been passed by the authorities of Herceg-Bosna. In addition, we asked that Mr. Hadziosmanovic stop representing the Muslims, the Bosniaks. We said that he should not continue to interpret their political goals any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, let me ask you, as a result of that meeting, was Mr. Hadziosmanovic removed as the president of the regional SDA and was Mr. Zijad Demirovic appointed in his place?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: There was a change at the regional level so that Mr. Zijad Demirovic headed the regional board, whereas Mr. Hadziosmanovic remained serving as the president of the SDA in Mostar, in the town of Mostar, although we asked openly that he be removed from that post too. But Mr. Izetbegovic did not follow our advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me move forward -- well, before I do that. Mr. Demirovic, did he then continue to be the regional president of the SDA for all of Herzegovina from approximately November of 1992 at least throughout -- at least throughout 1993 and sometime thereafter?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Up until the 9th of May, 1993, when he was captured in west -- Western Mostar and taken to the camp. He remained there almost a year, longer than any other prisoner, under terrible, very difficult circumstances. So that the HVO actually arrested its own partner, a member of the SDA, as well as his family, his son and so on. I don't need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we can move forward to January of 1993, did you and other leaders of the Muslim community learn in about the middle of that month that the HVO had issued a decision calling for all armies or forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to subordinate themselves to the HVO in certain territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew about that decree or appeal that was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, how that came to your attention?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: We learned it from the media. The HVO held its own press conferences and they made it known that -- made it public that they had issued an ultimatum, saying that all forces in that territory, which they considered to be Croatian, had to place themselves under the HVO command or else leave the area. Otherwise, the HVO would disarm them. That was the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look -- or for the witness to be shown, please, Exhibit P 01167. And when you have that document, sir, when you've had a chance to see what that is, can you tell the Judges what that document is and the circumstances of its preparation.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This document is the document prepared by representatives of all existing Muslim associations, and that was the greatest number that we have managed to gather around this issue so far. In this document, they express their concern due to threats that were to become reality, that were to be implemented in view of the contents of the ultimatum. Ultimatum spoke about disarming them, about expelling them. The conditions of the ultimatum were such that the Muslims could not agree to them. And this document will dispel any dilemmas concerning Hadziosmanovic. Even though we believed he wasn't going to sign it, he showed solidarity for our cause because the situation was a desperate one. We were a nation in our own state with our own army. We fought for the dignity of our own country. And the then paramilitary or illegal armed formations, and an illegal system, all of them together threatened to disarm the regular army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And there was no way we could have agreed to it. This document also mentions some other cases that were current at the time, and that led to the confrontation among these two nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registry to display the second page of the English version, please. And Mufti Smajkic, if you could direct your attention to the signature, the page that has the signatures on it. Do you have that? At the -- if I can direct your attention to the last part of paragraph numbered 6, starting with the language, "We resolutely deny --" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's just what I said. I have the English version here but I can understand. Basically, we refused to disarm or subordinate the army forcibly, by the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7, can you tell -- can you provide the Chamber with any additional information? When you say, "We resolutely reject the prejudicing of any political solutions and the transformation of proposals," what were you addressing in that situation, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This pertained to the planned provinces in Vance-Owen Plan, which were just a proposal, nothing but a proposal. This proposal probably suited the Croatian side, and they immediately took this proposal, accepted it, and wanted to implement it as the final agreement, as the final document, and this is something that we resolutely rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And looking further down the page, sir, did you sign this document and was your stamp or seal placed on the document?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did. I signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And also named in this document is Mr. Demirovic. Is that the man you were just referring to a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And then there are other persons who did as well, but you can't see it on the screen. Ismet Hadziosmanovic and representatives of other associations. There are other signatures in the original that you have, the original in Bosnian. You can see the names Zijad Demirovic, the regional committee, and then it says Faruk Cupina. There is the Ilmije Association, Adem Omerika. There is the Cultural Circle of Muslims, Ismet Hadziosmanovic is at the bottom to the left, and that concerns the municipal board of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the Registry could assist us to show to the general courtroom broadcast the signature page of the B/C/S document. If that's possible. There you have it. Can you see that now, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So these are the other signature and seals that you've told us about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In the interests of time, sir, could I ask the witness to please also be shown next Exhibit P 01167 -- I'm sorry, sorry, 1160. And as soon as you have that, sir, can you tell us, is that a document that was prepared essentially at the same time, involving many, not exactly the same, people, stating -- again expressing the concerns of the Muslim community at this time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It's a document drafted by the representatives of the same associations. It was done on the same day. In the document we had a look at prior to this one, entitled, "Charter," certain issues were raised in a more decisive manner, and they demonstrated the situation in which the Muslims found themselves and the threat of a conflict breaking out between the Muslims and the Croats, whereas in this case, this declaration is a summary of the same sort of problems, but the purpose of the declaration is to be made public, to the press and to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, just -- in the interests of time, let me just direct your attention to three particular parts of this document. If I can ask you to look, please, at -- toward the end of the third paragraph on the first page -- or in any event the third paragraph of the document, towards the end of that paragraph. You've mentioned to us earlier today in your testimony this issue about the liberation of various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the HVO. In paragraph 3 of this statement, are these concerns that you've raised and testified about indicated in this letter, in part?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We expressed our dissatisfaction because at the HVO press conferences, and in the press, they would emphasise the credit that should be given to the HVO for defending the territory, whereas the role of the army and of the Muslim forces was minimised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask, and I'm sorry -- still getting used myself to these electronic marvels - quote, unquote - but if we could move up to and show -- if we could highlight -- the Registry could assist in highlighting the end -- the language at the end of the third paragraph, please. Could I also ask you to -- in the -- in the fifth paragraph of the document, Mufti Smajkic, and it's quite a long paragraph, I'm afraid, but approximately halfway or a little more than halfway through that paragraph, you see the language where it talks about, "Unacceptable ultimatums about the subordination of our units." And again I'll ask the Registry to please assist, if they can, by focusing the electronic document on that language. In the interests of time, sir, while all that's happening, I'll just try to move forward as best we can. You referred to in this -- the document refers to "presenting unacceptable ultimatums." Is that a reference to the HVO ultimatum that had been issued on the 15th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's our response to that ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, on the last page of the document, or on the last paragraph of the document, do you -- can you also find the language, "These threats should be taken seriously as should the ultimatum presented to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina referring to 20 January." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, did the Muslim community receive any sort of satisfaction or response from the HVO withdrawing the ultimatums or indicating that the ultimatums in fact would not be enforced, or what if any response did you receive to these two documents?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive a response of any kind. Things only got worse. The situation was tense. There was an escalation. Other incidents occurred until this threat was carried out. There was another ultimatum in April and in May, 1993, the HVO attacked. That was four months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go to that. That was my next question to you. In about the middle of April, or in April, 1993, was a similar ultimatum issued by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's right. The same ultimatum was issued. The same ultimatum was issued once again. However, there were certain incidents that occurred and certain conflicts between the army and the HVO in Prozor and in Gornji Vakuf and elsewhere. So they had already started implementing their ideas and carrying out their threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The actions of the conflicts in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf, were these some of the actions that had taken place in connection with the January ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object again, Your Honour. I think unless there is a foundation laid, he's being asked to comment on facts that are not in evidence yet. So I suggest he can pose some questions, see if the gentleman has a foundation upon which he can answer this question, but I think here, and I'm going to be objecting to the leading. I keep hearing "in the interests of time" and Mr. Scott has been leading slightly. I've allowed it, but I think when we are getting into these sensitive areas, I'm going to insist on non-leading questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 114 of the transcript, line 21, the witness himself, before my question, talked about conflicts between the army and the HVO in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf and elsewhere. I did not suggest that to the witness, that was the witness's answer. If I can ask him if he can explain more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit more, sir, about the conflicts that you understood broke out in the areas of Prozor and Gornji Vakuf and elsewhere to the extent that you can now recall.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Naturally, I know that there was an offensive launched in January, 1993, when the ultimatum was issued. There was an offensive in Gornji Vakuf, but in Prozor in 1992 an attack was also carried out, and there was a terrible slaughter of civilians and members of the army. And there was no reason for this, and these were preparations for what was to subsequently happen. So the forces were probably trying to assess the situation and determine where they might meet with resistance or with even weak resistance. At that time they had already started carrying out their threats. But I have to say that Mostar was left for later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just in covering some of the events, then, during the spring of 1993, can you tell the Judges whether any vehicles were seized from you or members of your staff during this time period?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. My secretary's vehicle was seized. He was on his way to my office, and he came across a unit at the Rondo, whose commander was Misic, and he was the -- his vehicle was seized because he was the mufti's secretary. That was the only reason. He went to see the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment. When you say in your testimony, when you say "came across a unit," a unit of what army or military formation?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: An HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you referred to the commander by the name of Misic, do you remember -- do you recall Mr. Misic's first name?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Mladen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did anything else occur as part of this incident involving your secretary?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He went to see the commander himself and asked him to obtain the vehicle. He asked that I go to the military command to personally confirm that he was in fact my secretary and that the vehicle was his. He acted in a very brutal way. He even put his revolver in his mouth and insulted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say just now "he put his revolver in his mouth," who put his revolver in --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Commander Misic put the revolver in Mr. Mutevelic's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your secretary's mouth.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever get the car back, or did your secretary ever get the car back?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No. It was never returned. That same commander sent the military police to bring me in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The witness always spoke of a means of transport. You're now asking him and mentioning the word "car." Perhaps the witness ought to tell us what kind of a vehicle that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us the type of vehicle that the -- your secretary was using on that day and which was seized, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It was a small car. I think it was a Renault Clio.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the spring of 1993, sir, can you tell us if anything happened to Muslim intellectuals during this time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a campaign to detain Muslims, not only in Mostar but in Stolac and Capljina too. In February, March and April, between 200 and 300 intellectuals were imprisoned. They posed a threat in the eyes of the HVO. In fact they are aware of the reasons that they did this. But in any event, they were taken to concentration camps. They were maltreated there, and naturally, this had repercussions in the town of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What sort of -- excuse me, what sort of repercussions?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I know a lot of people from that period of time who went to sleep elsewhere because they couldn't sleep in their own homes. They sought shelter in places where they thought that the HVO police would not go to arrest them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you approach the Catholic bishop in Mostar, Bishop Peric, during this time, with any proposal? And when I say "this time," in approximately April, May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: We were in contact at all times. Although we didn't agree on everything, we remained in contact. I personally wanted to develop a good relationship with him, and to try and prevent these conflicts from breaking out, and this is demonstrated by all of our documents. So Mr. Demirovic, who died last year, together with some of my assistants, went to the cathedral and to the bishop's office and we asked him to issue an appeal together with me because there was a minor sniper war that was raging in April. The situation was a very confusing one. One didn't know whether a real conflict would break out or not. People would be intercepted and taken away. They would be kidnapped. So these people and I went to see the bishop, to tell him -- this was my proposal, because a line was already being established at the Bulevar, where -- from which fire was opened. There were sandbags placed there to create shelters from which machine-guns could be used. So I went to see the bishop to ask him to go and destroy the bunkers at the demarcation line. I said we should go there in uniform so that everyone can see us there because a great evil is being prepared. The bishop did not accept this suggestion. It doesn't mean that he supported the war but he simply said that that was not one of his duties, and he did not want to participate in anything of that kind. We then went to see Mr. Tolja [phoen] and we told him the same thing, we suggested the same thing, and the response was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So the record is clear, when you said a moment ago that you proposed to Bishop Peric that the two of you go together in uniform, was your proposal that the two of you go together in your clerical dress?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, so that they could recognise us and see that we were together at the line, to see us together at this location where they were establishing a line from which they had started opening fire. We wanted people to see us removing those sandbags that had been placed there so that people could take shelter behind them and open fire from those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in moving forward, sir, did you come to know that around this time, around the 9th of May, that President Izetbegovic had sent a letter to various of the leaders of the Muslim community in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have known that at the time because on the 9th of May a fierce attack was launched by the Croats against the Muslims. So I did not receive that result, but other individuals were engaged in this reconciliation mission. This is something I found out about later on, because I couldn't have received that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to see a copy of that letter at some time after the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It's only this summer that I found out about it. Commander Jaganac showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 02244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In order not to use time -- or to use it, you said in "this summer." Can you give the exact date? Because the summer isn't very old yet, if it has started at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was on the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, the attack. But the day when you learned, when you saw the letter. It says in the record, at least, "this summer."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The summer of 2005; last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you have Exhibit 02244 in front of you, sir, can you see, is that a copy of the letter that you did see in the summer of 2005?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's the letter, and I'm familiar with all these names that it was forwarded to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And your name was on the letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether the various people named on the first page of the letter, Mr. -- I'm not saying anyone specifically but just to name somebody for example: Mr. Omerbasic, Mr. Jaganac, Mr. Orucevic, any of these people around this time become involved in efforts to obtain a peace or a cease-fire between the Croats and the Muslims in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Four of these people went on a peace mission. I didn't go, but they had some contact with a delegation on the Croatian side. They represented the government. I don't know who this delegation was composed of, but I know that the result of the acts of this Commission for Reconciliation was that after the 9th of May, 1993, between eight and ten days later there was a temporary cessation of hostilities, and a high-ranking commission came from Zagreb, together with the Assembly speaker, at the time Mr. Seks. There were several foreign ambassadors who were part of the delegation. I believe that the Spanish and French ambassadors were there. I know that the Turkish ambassador was present. There was an ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mrs. Turkovic, and other representatives of international organisations were also present. They visited Mostar and I spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, sir, when you mention in your testimony just now Mr. Seks as being the speaker of an Assembly, which Assembly are you referring to, or of which Assembly was Mr. Seks the speaker at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He was the speaker of the Croatian Assembly, of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going to the 9th of May, you've already mentioned that an attack began that day. Can you just spend a couple of minutes, can't, I'm sure, address every detail, I'm afraid, but can you tell the Judges briefly what happened on the 9th of May, as far as what you experienced and saw occurring? I suppose let's start -- let me back up and ask you a question: Where were you on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I was in my home, in my house on the right bank, right next to the demarcation line which was established at the time. In the early morning hours, at dawn, there was fierce artillery fire, and attempts were made to expel the Muslim population and to expel people from their houses. People were expelled outside, They were in their pajamas or nightgowns, and they were driven off in various directions. Since my house is located at the demarcation line, I saw right next to my house, with my very own eyes, thousands of people who had been expelled. They had been woken up, and they were expelled. They left in tears, with their children, and they passed by my house and headed east. There was quite a large group that headed off in that direction. I'll never forget that event. There was crying, groaning, people were beside themselves. And while they were leaving, fire was opened on them from Hum and from other directions so that they would continue moving out. They continued in the direction of an overpass. The town was on fire. And the people said that they were taken away in several directions. But civilians and troops were taken to the stadium. Others were taken to other collection centres, to the Heliodrom, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who expelled these people, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The official policies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who took the people to, for instance, the Heliodrom? What armed force or what organisation?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The HVO units. Naturally, one could take a very long time in order to tell you about this, but I don't want to burden you with it. These are painful experiences. I can tell you that Jadran Topic, the president of the HVO, and the mayor, made an announcement on the radio, asking that all Muslims surrender and display white sheets, on their windows and everywhere else, as a sign of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to go on, in the next few days, what did you do, where did you stay during this time period, and what happened after that, in terms of your personal situation?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: As I told you, my house is on the right bank. On one side, there were the HVO units, which were responsible for this terrible, fierce fire. On the other side were the units of the BH army. So I found myself in the crossfire. The army at the time believed that the HVO units had entered the houses where I and my neighbours were, so that that entire time, from morning to night, I was unable to go outside. It was quite ironic that the BH army could have killed me, because they had been told that the HVO had occupied those houses. Fortunately, they recognised me. I went there and I read, because on the previous day, on the 9th day, we received the letter from Mr. Izetbegovic, removing Mr. Hadziosmanovic from his post. So I went to an improvised studio with a limited range for broadcast, and I personally read out this announcement on the removal of Mr. Hadziosmanovic, and also asking the people to put up some resistance, as much as possible, not to take this attitude of slaves by displaying white sheets or white flags, but, rather, to protect their honour, protect their Mostar, and protect the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn during this time that a -- on the 9th or 10th of May 1993, that an Islamic cleric, an imam named Salem Mezit was killed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. His house is on the other side of the boulevard, away from my house. His family was expelled and they came to see me and they brought me the sad news, namely that the HVO units, whose house -- or, rather, that the HVO units came to his house, which was across from the Catholic church, and he was taken out, together with eight Muslims from the house, in a brutal way, and shot, executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, if the witness can be shown Exhibit P 02493, and I'm also going to ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 02565. Sir, in the interests of time, I'm just going to ask you, when you see these two documents, are these letters of protest that you wrote to various people indicated on the face of the documents, about the murder of Salem Mezit?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If the witness could be shown, then, also 2565. And is that a second letter that you wrote, addressed to such people as UNPROFOR, ECMM, ICRC, the HVO, and the bishop in Mostar, that you wrote concerning the killing of Imam Mezit?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we continue on, sir, you made reference to this meeting, or you made reference to meetings involving Mr. Seks and various ambassadors. Can you tell the Judges, as part of that meeting or as a part of any meeting that was related to this particular meeting, perhaps a series of meetings, did you have any involvement or dealings around that time with a man named Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic was in that delegation, together with -- yes, I failed to mention this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't see you. You were hidden behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that this witness n-- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe this witness is about to give evidence of what happened during the visit of a delegation from Zagreb to East Mostar on the 19th of May, 1993, when Mr. Pusic was present. I wish to raise an objection on behalf of my client to this evidence on the basis that we were first given notice of this evidence at a very late stage, indeed on Monday of this week. If I may just provide some background so that the Court can understand the nature of my objection in more detail. This witness did not mention this incident or the fact that he met my client when he gave his statement, his first statement, to the Prosecution. This statement was taken from the witness on the 23rd to 29th of September, 1999. On Monday of this week, we were given advance notice that there was new evidence elicited from this witness and that we presume was obtained after the Prosecution had proofed this witness earlier this week. Our submission is that this new evidence causes prejudice to the Defence because we have not had any opportunity to verify the events that this witness, we assume, is about to describe. Had we been given proper notice, then, for instance, we could have conducted various inquiries, including attempts to locate, identify and interview other witnesses who were present during the course of this incident, inquiries to try and identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understood. Mr. Scott, what do you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree largely with what my colleague has said. It was indeed not in the prior statement, and that is the very reason that on first learning of this information earlier this week, on Monday, that it was immediately disclosed to the Defence counsel, including counsel for Mr. Pusic. It was simply not known to us before and, as we indicated before, in the context of preparing and talking to these witnesses, it's not at all uncommon - for better or worse - but not at all uncommon for the witness to say something that may not have been said on a prior occasion. So it was -- all I can say is it was disclosed absolutely as soon as it became known to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But Mr. Scott, the general rule is that whenever you examine a witness on the basis of a written statement provided to the Defence, your questions have to focus, have to pertain, to the contents of that statement. You may not raise issues or put questions not included in the statement. If you -- another matter is when you ask something mentioned in the statement and then the witness gives you new information. Then it's a different matter. Then you can clarify this, if you obtain this new information in this manner. But to do what you are doing, to start raising an issue that can be prejudicial to Defence because they did not have a chance to prepare for that is not going to be allowed. Please continue with your examination, but skip this topic, because there are many more other important aspects which need to be covered, and you have less than an hour available to you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, so far, Your Honour, I've indicated it would be four and a half hours and our records indicate that so far I've used a little over three hours. I'm sure the Registry can confirm the time usage. And while I'm very concerned about the usage of time, Your Honour, I must make a brief response. I don't believe the ICTY jurisprudence or practice is, with all due respect, what Your Honour has indicated. The witness is not limited to examination on questions put in prior statements. The witness can be asked about anything of relevance to the case. There is a separate disclosure issue and, of course, disclosure has to be made as soon as possible, which was done in this case. It could not have been possibly been done any sooner. Secondly, as to the -- what you indicate, that if it comes up in the context of putting questions to a witness about his statement, his prior statement, then you've indicated that that is allowable. That's exactly what happened in this situation. The context of talking to Mufti Smajkic and about the events in Mostar during May, 1993, and talking about those things, he also related to us, for the first time, this other additional piece of information. And I don't know what more we can do except to disclose that information as soon as it comes to our attention. So I would like to present that evidence to the Court. If the Court is not going to allow us to do that, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may continue. However, you can raise this issue, given that the role of Mr. Pusic is relevant to this witness, and has to do -- is relevant for the indictment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: May I raise just two more issues in response to some of the paints made by my learned colleague? Mr. President, this evidence could have been elicited from this witness, in our submission, had he simply been asked in 1999, "Have you ever met Mr. Pusic?" Had he been asked that, we anticipate that he may have or would be likely to have given the testimony that the Prosecution now intend to adduce from him. Secondly, can we point out to the Tribunal that this witness is no stranger to the Prosecution, nor is he a stranger to Mr. Scott. I have been informed that this witness gave evidence for three days in 2001 in another set of proceedings when Mr. Scott was the lead counsel for the Prosecution. In these circumstances, this Court, in our submission, is entitled to ask why was this witness never asked prior to attending court for these proceedings whether he had ever come into contact with our client. Mr. President, I'm not going to repeat my submission, but it remains the case, as far as the Defence of Mr. Pusic is concerned, that the late submission of this evidence causes us severe prejudice, and we would ask the Court to consider once again whether it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you heard what was just said now. This witness is somebody whom you know well because apparently you examined him back in 2001. The Defence wonders how come, in 1999, the investigator did not put the relevant question to him about the persons present here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, in terms of the second part, again I agree with my colleague. I absolutely have never made any secret, and on it's on the public record, that I examined this witness in the Tuta/Stela case. There is no attempt at any sleight of hand about that. Yes, indeed, I did. And in that particular case, the involvement of Mr. Pusic was not relevant. The case was involved against Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic. So there was absolutely no reason at that particular time for me to raise questions about Mr. Pusic. In fact, very well might have, I suppose, gotten an objection from counsel or from the Court at that time that I was going into something irrelevant. So there was a simply no point in me eliciting that information from the witness in 2001, some five years ago. As to what happened in 1999, Your Honours, I'm afraid again that counsel's questions or position is premised on a rather artificial notion of the investigator process. It may very well have been that at that particular moment, this investigator, I don't know, recall off-hand who took the statement - I don't have the statement in front of me - may or may not have been thinking about Mr. Pusic or had Mr. Pusic in mind at the time. Could have been any number of things. I assure you that any statement can be reviewed and found things that were not asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Listen, I will resolve this issue in the following way: I will personally address the witness. Sir, see, there are a number of persons in this courtroom. In the previous years, have you ever had occasion to meet any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In May, when this high level delegation from the Republic of Croatia came, together with the representatives of the international community, and when they came to Mostar and when the fire ceased on both sides, and the delegation crossed into East Mostar, I saw them together with Commander Pasalic. It simply did not occur to me to mention this earlier. Nobody told me this. But now, given that these persons are here, it triggered my memory, and I remembered this instance. Mr. Berislav Pusic was part of that delegation, and this remained vivid in my memory. I will never forget it, because we visited an improvised hospital. Then we went on to visit a camp and a basement from which the people from West Mostar had been expelled. It was a dark room. Those were dark basement premises, without any furniture. A lot of sick persons were lying on the floor. I don't need to spend much time talking about this but let me just give you a detail about something that Mr. Pusic did, addressing these long-suffering people. He said, "Do you know why you find yourselves in this unfortunate situation? Who is to blame for that?" People just looked at him because they knew who was to blame for that. And then he turned himself to the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Pasalic, and said, "He is to blame for this. He is the culprit." This is what I told the Prosecutor. I told him about this episode so that it is recorded. There was this constant policy to do something that was bad and to blame the other side for that. It wasn't enough that these people suffered terrible destiny but they also had to blame for that the political and military leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you are now telling us that Mr. Pusic, when talking to these people, told them that it was Mr. Pasalic who was to blame for the situation in which they found themselves. What about this delegation? Had it come from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about Mr. Pusic? He's a citizen of Croatia. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was an official of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and he was in charge of exchanges of prisoners. That's what he did within the HVO, together with the representatives of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I put a very specific question to you. You said that a delegation had come from Croatia. You could have said a delegation from Switzerland. When you say that a delegation from Switzerland came, then we assume that its members were from Switzerland, and when you say that the delegation came from Croatia, then we assume that it comprised Croats. So who was in that delegation? Was it only Croats from Croatia and Croats from Mostar or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Representatives of the Republic of Croatia were in that delegation, as well as the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Pusic was a representative of Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that delegation was also the lady who was the ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the clarification. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the same or analogous line, when the president asked you whether you had seen anybody who is in this room before, you said, "I saw them." Did you see someone else before, except Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had occasion to meet Mr. Prlic and Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's all for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott. Yes, Mr. Sahota?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may I ask the leave of the Court, if necessary, if at a later stage, information should come to light that is not available to the Defence team for Mr. Pusic today, may we have the Court's permission to ask for this witness to be recalled, should that situation arise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Certainly. Of course. Please go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Just seeing where we left off, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward to the situation in Mostar in the summer and fall of 1993, can you briefly tell the Judges about any sniping that you were familiar with or that you can tell the Judges about.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: After the 9th of May; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: In the period after the 9th of May, the Muslims found themselves in a total encirclement, in a small area. They were constantly shelled, fired upon, both from artillery and snipers. I can tell you very briefly that the War Presidency, which was established at the time on the left bank, because people were dying in great numbers, issued a decision restricting or banning any movement during the day. So that all activities that were necessary had to be conducted at night, and people had to swap day for night, even though many were killed at night too. We had serious difficulties in burying those who were killed, the victims. We had to do it at night, we had to hide because buildings, we had to find sufficient space in parks and other areas to bury the people who were killed. Snipers targeted everything that moved. The favourite target of snipers were places where people came to have a drink of water or just gathered for any other purpose. We, in the Islamic community, were fully aware of this and we told the people they were not allowed to go to the damaged religious facilities, because those were also targeted by snipers, they were quite popular with the snipers. And this was a chaotic situation. This was an entry into hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 02586. And while that's being done, Mufti Smajkic, can I ask you, did you ever approach, during this -- the circumstances you've just related to us in the last few minutes, did you ever ask the HVO to allow a cease-fire or a time of relative peace, in order to celebrate certain Islamic holidays?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: There is the document here. We sent this to Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Topic, and we sent a request to them by UNPROFOR. We requested that Bajram, on the 1st of June, 1993, be celebrated in peace. We hoped that this peace would be extended after the end of Bajram, which is our most important religious holiday. This was a reason we would always take advantage of. We would take advantage of any opportunity to put an end to the hostilities and put an end to the killing and destruction of infrastructure. We tried to spread this idea among people until they understood us. As I have said, after Bajram, we wanted this cease-fire to be extended, and the document that you have before you relates to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
